**Today's date: 2026-05-30 (UTC).**

## Research context

We are generating ideas in the area of: **Target: AAAI 2026
Track: Machine Learning / Knowledge Representation and Reasoning

Direction: Trace the complete computational circuit governing RAG evidence integration vs. override in open-weight LLMs, mapping causal interactions between retrieval heads, parametric memory components, copy suppression mechanisms, and FFN layers. Use the discovered circuit to design principled, multi-point inference-time interventions that outperform existing heuristic steering methods (SpARE, CoRect, ContextFocus) on knowledge-conflict benchmarks.

Seed Papers:
- ReDeEP (ICLR 2025) — Identifies Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads as key components but stops at component-level; no circuit tracing
- Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality (ICLR 2025) — Identifies <5% of heads carry retrieval signal; universal across model families; but no interaction with parametric circuits
- Taming Knowledge Conflicts / JuICE (ICML 2025) — Discovers superposition in attention heads (both memory and context); proposes test-time intervention; complicates clean head-type dichotomy but remains head-level
- CoRect (arXiv 2025) — Discovers flip phenomenon (56% of conflict cases); deep FFN layers suppress correct answers; intervention is additive patching without circuit diagnosis
- Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers (NeurIPS 2024) — Provides circuit discovery methodology for factual recall; not applied to RAG
- CD-T: Efficient Automated Circuit Discovery (ICLR 2025) — Enables circuit discovery in seconds; 97% ROC AUC; key enabling tool
- SpARE (NAACL 2025) — SAE-based steering under knowledge conflicts; +10% EM; heuristic target selection
- Atlas of In-Context Learning (NeurIPS 2025) — Separates in-context vs parametric heads; 94% AUC linear probe; but no causal interaction mapping

Known Gaps:
- No end-to-end circuit has been traced connecting retrieval heads → FFN layers → copy suppression → output in RAG, comparing success vs failure cases
- JUICE shows heads operate in superposition (both memory and context), but no work has traced how this superposition resolves across layers and through FFN interactions
- The flip phenomenon (CoRect: correct answers appear mid-layers then get suppressed) has no circuit-level causal explanation
- Existing interventions (SpARE, CoRect, ContextFocus, JuICE) select targets heuristically or statistically, not via causal circuit analysis; no multi-point coordinated intervention exists

Theoretical Anchor: The promote-suppress-iterate mechanism (Yan & Jia, EMNLP 2025) provides a theoretical framework — MLPs promote all candidate answers while attention suppresses alternatives iteratively. In RAG, this mechanism should create a specific circuit pathology: retrieval heads promote context-derived answers, but parametric MLPs re-promote stored answers in deeper layers, and copy suppression heads (which operate via general suppression, not selective) inadvertently suppress context-derived tokens. The flip phenomenon is a direct observable consequence of this circuit pathology.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours
- Models: Llama-3.1-8B (primary), Gemma-2-9B (validation)
- Tools: CD-T, TransformerLens, pyvene, attribution patching
- Timeline: 10-12 weeks to AAAI August 2026 deadline

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: In RAG, evidence override is caused by a specific circuit pathology where parametric MLPs in deep layers re-assert stored answers after retrieval heads have already injected context-derived answers — and this pathology can be surgically repaired.
- [x] Why not obvious: JUICE shows heads are in superposition (not cleanly separable), so you can't just prune memory heads. You need full circuit tracing to find where the parametric signal actually dominates, which requires the promote-suppress-iterate lens applied to RAG specifically.
- [x] Baseline fear test: Simple baselines (prune top-k memory heads, boost top-k retrieval heads) exist (Jin et al. 2024, IRCAN). Circuit-informed intervention must show that selecting targets via causal analysis yields better targets than statistical/heuristic selection. The multi-point coordination (boost + suppress simultaneously at circuit-identified layers) is what baselines cannot do.
- [x] Information exploited: The full causal interaction graph between components that existing methods treat in isolation. Specifically, which FFN neurons in which layers re-assert parametric answers AFTER retrieval heads have already injected context, and which copy suppression heads inadvertently suppress context-derived tokens.

Avoid:
- Replicating ReDeEP at larger scale (component identification without circuit tracing)
- Assuming clean retrieval-head vs memory-head separation (JUICE refutes this; must account for superposition)
- Pure interpretability without intervention (AAAI reviewers will ask 'so what?')
- Ignoring the flip phenomenon as validation (it's the most mechanistically informative empirical finding)
- Over-claiming circuit completeness (circuits at 7B may be distributed; frame contributions carefully)**

# Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head

**Paper:** "Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head" (arxiv: 2310.04625)
**Authors:** Callum McDougall, Arthur Conmy, Cody Rushing, Thomas McGrath, Neel Nanda
**Venues:** BlackboxNLP 2024 (EMNLP Workshop, Miami, Florida, Nov 2024, pp. 337-363); also published in *Patterns* (Cell Press), accepted January 13, 2025. Originally submitted to ICLR 2024 on OpenReview (forum id: g8oaZRhDcf). Research conducted as part of SERI MATS 2023 under Neel Nanda's mentorship.
**Citations:** ~60 (per MATS page)
**Interactive visualizations:** https://copy-suppression.streamlit.app/

---

## Full Abstract

> "We present a single attention head in GPT-2 Small that has one main role across the entire training distribution. If components in earlier layers predict a certain token, and this token appears earlier in the context, the head suppresses it: we call this copy suppression. Attention Head 10.7 (L10H7) suppresses naive copying behavior which improves overall model calibration. This explains why multiple prior works studying certain narrow tasks found negative heads that systematically favored the wrong answer. We uncover the mechanism that the Negative Heads use for copy suppression with weights-based evidence and are able to explain 76.9% of the impact of L10H7 in GPT-2 Small. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive description of the complete role of a component in a language model to date. One major effect of copy suppression is its role in self-repair. Self-repair refers to how ablating crucial model components results in downstream neural network parts compensating for this ablation."

---

## The Copy Suppression Mechanism: Three-Step Process

Copy suppression operates through three sequential steps:

### Step 1: Prior Copying
Components in earlier layers (e.g., induction heads, previous-token heads) predict a token that already appears somewhere earlier in the context. These earlier components build up logit predictions via the residual stream.

### Step 2: Attention (QK Circuit)
L10H7 detects that the model is currently predicting a token that matches one appearing earlier in context. The QK circuit determines *when* the head activates. The authors analyze the matrix:

**W_U . W_QK^{L10H7} . MLP0(W_E)**

The diagonal dominance analysis shows **95.72% of diagonal elements rank as largest in their respective rows**, meaning L10H7 attends most strongly when the query token (what the model currently predicts) matches the key token (a candidate token in context). Crucially, this is not merely "same-token matching" -- the QK circuit specifically matches *predictions* (from the residual stream / logit lens) to contextual tokens, not raw embeddings. The authors confirmed this by comparing against a baseline using raw embeddings for both queries and keys, which showed substantially lower diagonal rank dominance.

### Step 3: Suppression (OV Circuit)
Once attending to a source token, L10H7 writes a negative contribution to that token's logit, suppressing its prediction. The OV circuit is analyzed via:

**W_U . W_OV^{L10H7} . MLP0(W_E)**

Key finding: **84.70% of vocabulary tokens have their diagonal elements (self-suppression) ranked among the top 10 most negative values in their respective columns.** This means the head systematically writes negative logits for the token it attends to. In practice on OpenWebText data, **78.24% of high-attention (source, destination) token pairs** showed the source token among the 10 most suppressed tokens.

### Illustrative Example
With the input "All's fair in love and ___", earlier layers (induction heads) predict "love" because it appeared before. L10H7 detects this prediction, attends back to the earlier occurrence of "love," and writes a negative logit contribution for "love," thus allowing the correct prediction "war" to surface. When L10H7 is ablated, the model incorrectly predicts "...love and love."

---

## How Copy Suppression Reduces Model Loss

- **Mean ablating L10H7 increases model loss**, confirming it plays a beneficial role.
- Approximately **90% of L10H7's impact occurs via the direct effect** to final logits (not through indirect effects on later layers).
- The head improves **model calibration** by reducing overconfidence in copied tokens. Calibration metrics show L10H7 most reduces entropy and overconfidence.
- Behavioral sampling from the **top 5% of completions** where L10H7 has greatest impact showed **80% matched copy suppression criteria**: (1) a high-confidence copying prediction by earlier layers, (2) attention to that token's prior occurrence, and (3) reduced logits on that token.

---

## Copy Suppression-Preserving Ablation (CSPA) -- Experimental Methodology

The central methodological innovation is CSPA, an ablation that preserves *only* the identified copy suppression mechanism while removing all other head functionality. This allows quantifying how much of the head's behavior is explained by copy suppression alone.

CSPA has two components:

1. **OV ablation:** Projects head outputs onto unembedding vectors for attended tokens, retaining only the negative components (suppressive effects). Positive (non-suppressive) contributions are zeroed out.

2. **QK ablation:** Mean-ablates the residual stream input to the head except for the **top 5% of tokens** with the highest logit lens predictions at each destination position. This ensures the head only attends to tokens the model is actively predicting.

### Quantification Metric
The KL divergence recovery metric:

**Recovery = 1 - (D_CSPA / D_MA)**

Where D_CSPA is the average KL divergence between the model's output with CSPA applied vs. the full model, and D_MA is the same divergence under mean ablation (complete removal).

### Results
- **CSPA recovers 76.9%** of L10H7's total KL divergence effect
- OV-only ablation: **81.1%** recovery
- QK-only ablation: **95.2%** recovery
- In the **top 1 percentile** (where mean ablation is most destructive), recovery reaches **88.1%**
- The largest effects cluster in the top percentile, meaning copy suppression is especially important exactly where the head matters most

---

## Semantic Copy Suppression

Beyond strict token matching, L10H7 performs "semantic copy suppression." When attending to a token, it suppresses not just exact matches but **semantically related variants**:
- Capitalization variants (e.g., "the" / "The")
- Plural forms
- Morphological roots
- Tokenization artifacts (different BPE splits of the same word)

The authors found **90% of cases** where the most-suppressed token differed from the attended source involved semantic relatedness, despite moderate cosine similarity (average 0.520).

---

## Anti-Copying Behavior and Negative Heads

The paper provides a unified explanation for "negative heads" -- attention heads previously observed in narrow-task studies (like Indirect Object Identification) that systematically appeared to favor wrong answers. The key insight is that these heads are not "wrong" -- they are performing copy suppression across the full distribution, and this manifests as anti-copying on narrow tasks.

The distinction between head types:
- **Negative heads** (including L10H7): Increase attention to copied tokens and suppress their logits (write negative contributions)
- **Backup heads**: Decrease attention to copied tokens and increase logits on those tokens (compensatory)

---

## Self-Repair

Copy suppression creates self-repair dynamics. When preceding components (e.g., induction heads, Name Mover Heads in IOI) are ablated:
- There is nothing incorrect to suppress, so copy suppression naturally deactivates
- This "passive" deactivation means downstream loss from ablation is partially compensated automatically
- On the Indirect Object Identification task, negative heads (including L10H7) explain **39% of overall self-repair behavior**

However, self-repair depends on more than just the unembedding direction -- a **perpendicular component** carries substantial importance, indicating the mechanism is more complex than simple directional encoding.

---

## Function Word Exception

Approximately **7.4% of tokens** escape strong suppression. These are predominantly function words ("of," "that," "their," "as," etc.) which show substantially smaller unembedding magnitudes. The authors suggest these words rarely benefit from copy suppression given their high contextual frequency.

---

## Limitations

The authors acknowledge several constraints:

1. **Query-side inputs incompletely explained:** The query computation feeding into self-repair heads remains not fully understood.
2. **GPT-2 Small only:** Results center on GPT-2 Small; generalization to larger models remains unclear and proved inconsistent in initial checks.
3. **Perpendicular component unexplained:** The component perpendicular to unembedding directions appears causally important for self-repair but lacks a full mechanistic description.
4. **No training dynamics explanation:** The paper explains *what* copy suppression does but not *why* it emerges during training.
5. **KL divergence metric limitations:** KL divergence alone proved insufficient as a metric; additional behavioral analysis was needed.

Three speculative theories for *why* copy suppression forms:
- Reducing overconfidence (supported by calibration metrics)
- Suppressing naive copying as an "update property" of contextual tokens
- Correcting artifacts from tied embedding matrices (supported by findings in models with tied embeddings)

---

## Reviewer Comments

The paper was submitted to **ICLR 2024** (OpenReview forum id: g8oaZRhDcf) but the reviews are not publicly accessible through the current OpenReview interface -- the pages only show metadata without review content. It was subsequently accepted to **BlackboxNLP 2024** (EMNLP Workshop, OpenReview forum id: 5Hd6813x3U) and published in **Patterns** (Cell Press, accepted January 13, 2025). Unfortunately, the actual reviewer text for none of these venues was accessible through web fetching. # Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head

**Paper:** "Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head" (arxiv: 2310.04625)
**Authors:** Callum McDougall, Arthur Conmy, Cody Rushing, Thomas McGrath, Neel Nanda
**Venues:** BlackboxNLP 2024 (EMNLP Workshop, Miami, Florida, Nov 2024, pp. 337-363); also published in *Patterns* (Cell Press), accepted January 13, 2025. Originally submitted to ICLR 2024 on OpenReview (forum id: g8oaZRhDcf). Research conducted as part of SERI MATS 2023 under Neel Nanda's mentorship.
**Citations:** ~60 (per MATS page)
**Interactive visualizations:** https://copy-suppression.streamlit.app/

---

## Full Abstract

> "We present a single attention head in GPT-2 Small that has one main role across the entire training distribution. If components in earlier layers predict a certain token, and this token appears earlier in the context, the head suppresses it: we call this copy suppression. Attention Head 10.7 (L10H7) suppresses naive copying behavior which improves overall model calibration. This explains why multiple prior works studying certain narrow tasks found negative heads that systematically favored the wrong answer. We uncover the mechanism that the Negative Heads use for copy suppression with weights-based evidence and are able to explain 76.9% of the impact of L10H7 in GPT-2 Small. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive description of the complete role of a component in a language model to date. One major effect of copy suppression is its role in self-repair. Self-repair refers to how ablating crucial model components results in downstream neural network parts compensating for this ablation."

---

## The Copy Suppression Mechanism: Three-Step Process

Copy suppression operates through three sequential steps:

### Step 1: Prior Copying
Components in earlier layers (e.g., induction heads, previous-token heads) predict a token that already appears somewhere earlier in the context. These earlier components build up logit predictions via the residual stream.

### Step 2: Attention (QK Circuit)
L10H7 detects that the model is currently predicting a token that matches one appearing earlier in context. The QK circuit determines *when* the head activates. The authors analyze the matrix:

**W_U . W_QK^{L10H7} . MLP0(W_E)**

The diagonal dominance analysis shows **95.72% of diagonal elements rank as largest in their respective rows**, meaning L10H7 attends most strongly when the query token (what the model currently predicts) matches the key token (a candidate token in context). Crucially, this is not merely "same-token matching" -- the QK circuit specifically matches *predictions* (from the residual stream / logit lens) to contextual tokens, not raw embeddings. The authors confirmed this by comparing against a baseline using raw embeddings for both queries and keys, which showed substantially lower diagonal rank dominance.

### Step 3: Suppression (OV Circuit)
Once attending to a source token, L10H7 writes a negative contribution to that token's logit, suppressing its prediction. The OV circuit is analyzed via:

**W_U . W_OV^{L10H7} . MLP0(W_E)**

Key finding: **84.70% of vocabulary tokens have their diagonal elements (self-suppression) ranked among the top 10 most negative values in their respective columns.** This means the head systematically writes negative logits for the token it attends to. In practice on OpenWebText data, **78.24% of high-attention (source, destination) token pairs** showed the source token among the 10 most suppressed tokens.

### Illustrative Example
With the input "All's fair in love and ___", earlier layers (induction heads) predict "love" because it appeared before. L10H7 detects this prediction, attends back to the earlier occurrence of "love," and writes a negative logit contribution for "love," thus allowing the correct prediction "war" to surface. When L10H7 is ablated, the model incorrectly predicts "...love and love."

---

## How Copy Suppression Reduces Model Loss

- **Mean ablating L10H7 increases model loss**, confirming it plays a beneficial role.
- Approximately **90% of L10H7's impact occurs via the direct effect** to final logits (not through indirect effects on later layers).
- The head improves **model calibration** by reducing overconfidence in copied tokens. Calibration metrics show L10H7 most reduces entropy and overconfidence.
- Behavioral sampling from the **top 5% of completions** where L10H7 has greatest impact showed **80% matched copy suppression criteria**: (1) a high-confidence copying prediction by earlier layers, (2) attention to that token's prior occurrence, and (3) reduced logits on that token.

---

## Copy Suppression-Preserving Ablation (CSPA) -- Experimental Methodology

The central methodological innovation is CSPA, an ablation that preserves *only* the identified copy suppression mechanism while removing all other head functionality. This allows quantifying how much of the head's behavior is explained by copy suppression alone.

CSPA has two components:

1. **OV ablation:** Projects head outputs onto unembedding vectors for attended tokens, retaining only the negative components (suppressive effects). Positive (non-suppressive) contributions are zeroed out.

2. **QK ablation:** Mean-ablates the residual stream input to the head except for the **top 5% of tokens** with the highest logit lens predictions at each destination position. This ensures the head only attends to tokens the model is actively predicting.

### Quantification Metric
The KL divergence recovery metric:

**Recovery = 1 - (D_CSPA / D_MA)**

Where D_CSPA is the average KL divergence between the model's output with CSPA applied vs. the full model, and D_MA is the same divergence under mean ablation (complete removal).

### Results
- **CSPA recovers 76.9%** of L10H7's total KL divergence effect
- OV-only ablation: **81.1%** recovery
- QK-only ablation: **95.2%** recovery
- In the **top 1 percentile** (where mean ablation is most destructive), recovery reaches **88.1%**
- The largest effects cluster in the top percentile, meaning copy suppression is especially important exactly where the head matters most

---

## Semantic Copy Suppression

Beyond strict token matching, L10H7 performs "semantic copy suppression." When attending to a token, it suppresses not just exact matches but **semantically related variants**:
- Capitalization variants (e.g., "the" / "The")
- Plural forms
- Morphological roots
- Tokenization artifacts (different BPE splits of the same word)

The authors found **90% of cases** where the most-suppressed token differed from the attended source involved semantic relatedness, despite moderate cosine similarity (average 0.520).

---

## Anti-Copying Behavior and Negative Heads

The paper provides a unified explanation for "negative heads" -- attention heads previously observed in narrow-task studies (like Indirect Object Identification) that systematically appeared to favor wrong answers. The key insight is that these heads are not "wrong" -- they are performing copy suppression across the full distribution, and this manifests as anti-copying on narrow tasks.

The distinction between head types:
- **Negative heads** (including L10H7): Increase attention to copied tokens and suppress their logits (write negative contributions)
- **Backup heads**: Decrease attention to copied tokens and increase logits on those tokens (compensatory)

---

## Self-Repair

Copy suppression creates self-repair dynamics. When preceding components (e.g., induction heads, Name Mover Heads in IOI) are ablated:
- There is nothing incorrect to suppress, so copy suppression naturally deactivates
- This "passive" deactivation means downstream loss from ablation is partially compensated automatically
- On the Indirect Object Identification task, negative heads (including L10H7) explain **39% of overall self-repair behavior**

However, self-repair depends on more than just the unembedding direction -- a **perpendicular component** carries substantial importance, indicating the mechanism is more complex than simple directional encoding.

---

## Function Word Exception

Approximately **7.4% of tokens** escape strong suppression. These are predominantly function words ("of," "that," "their," "as," etc.) which show substantially smaller unembedding magnitudes. The authors suggest these words rarely benefit from copy suppression given their high contextual frequency.

---

## Limitations

The authors acknowledge several constraints:

1. **Query-side inputs incompletely explained:** The query computation feeding into self-repair heads remains not fully understood.
2. **GPT-2 Small only:** Results center on GPT-2 Small; generalization to larger models remains unclear and proved inconsistent in initial checks.
3. **Perpendicular component unexplained:** The component perpendicular to unembedding directions appears causally important for self-repair but lacks a full mechanistic description.
4. **No training dynamics explanation:** The paper explains *what* copy suppression does but not *why* it emerges during training.
5. **KL divergence metric limitations:** KL divergence alone proved insufficient as a metric; additional behavioral analysis was needed.

Three speculative theories for *why* copy suppression forms:
- Reducing overconfidence (supported by calibration metrics)
- Suppressing naive copying as an "update property" of contextual tokens
- Correcting artifacts from tied embedding matrices (supported by findings in models with tied embeddings)

---

## Reviewer Comments

The paper was submitted to **ICLR 2024** (OpenReview forum id: g8oaZRhDcf) but the reviews are not publicly accessible through the current OpenReview interface -- the pages only show metadata without review content. It was subsequently accepted to **BlackboxNLP 2024** (EMNLP Workshop, OpenReview forum id: 5Hd6813x3U) and published in **Patterns** (Cell Press, accepted January 13, 2025). Unfortunately, the actual reviewer text for none of these venues was accessible through web fetching. The ICLR submission appears to have been rejected given the paper's subsequent publication at a workshop venue, but the specific reviewer scores and comments could not be retrieved.

---

- Conducted at **SERI MATS 2023** by fellows Callum McDougall and Cody Rushing, with Arthur Conmy, mentored by Neel Nanda and Tom McGrath.
- The LessWrong post discusses research methodology insights: the importance of developing adversarial experiments early, recognizing metric limitations, separating experimental and writing phases, and using visual organization (Excalidraw) for hypothesis tracking.
- Community discussion on LessWrong suggested using **Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs)** to further decompose which representational dimensions the suppression mechanism operates on.

## Research Report: "How Do LLMs Acquire New Knowledge? A Knowledge Circuits Perspective on Continual Pre-Training"

**Authors:** Yixin Ou, Yunzhi Yao, Ningyu Zhang, Hui Jin, Jiacheng Sun, Shumin Deng, Zhenguo Li, Huajun Chen
**Venue:** Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025 (pages 19889-19913), Vienna, Austria, July 2025
**ACL Anthology ID:** 2025.findings-acl.1021
**Code:** https://github.com/zjunlp/DynamicKnowledgeCircuits

---

### Full Abstract

> "Despite exceptional capabilities in knowledge-intensive tasks, Large Language Models (LLMs) face a critical gap in understanding how they internalize new knowledge, particularly how to structurally embed acquired knowledge in their neural computations. We address this issue through the lens of knowledge circuit evolution, identifying computational subgraphs that facilitate knowledge storage and processing. Our systematic analysis of circuit evolution throughout continual pre-training reveals several key findings: (1) the acquisition of new knowledge is influenced by its relevance to pre-existing knowledge; (2) the evolution of knowledge circuits exhibits a distinct phase shift from formation to optimization; (3) the evolution of knowledge circuits follows a deep-to-shallow pattern."

---

### Knowledge Circuits: Definition and Discovery

**Definition:** Knowledge circuits are defined as *sparse computational subgraphs* within LLMs where "computations are most relevant to the whole model's behaviour on the specific task." They consist of selected **nodes** (attention heads, MLPs) and **edges** (connections between components) necessary for knowledge storage and retrieval.

**Discovery Algorithm -- EAP-IG:** The paper uses **Edge Attribution Patching with Integrated Gradients (EAP-IG)** to identify circuits. The importance score for each edge is:

S(e) = (z'_u - z_u) x (1/m) sum(dL/dz_v)

where z_u and z'_u are clean and corrupted activations, with m=5 integrated gradient steps. Edges are normalized, and the top edges are retained such that they achieve at least **70% of the whole model's performance**.

**Edge retention counts by model:**
- GPT-2 Small: 8,000 edges retained
- GPT-2 Medium: 20,000 edges
- TinyLlama-1.1B: 50,000 edges
- Phi-1.5: 50,000 edges

**Validation:** 300 randomly sampled examples per knowledge type/frequency combination. Corrupted inputs are independently sampled from the corpus, matched to subject token length. The loss function is L(x) = -M(x), where M is the logit difference metric (correct attribute logit minus corrupted attribute logit).

**Implementation:** Built on modified versions of the TransformerLens library (Nanda & Bloom, 2022) and the EAP-IG library (Hanna et al., 2024).

---

### Models Used

Four decoder-only Transformer architectures:

| Model | Parameters | Nodes | Edges | Epochs | Batch Size |
|-------|-----------|-------|-------|--------|------------|
| GPT-2 Small | 124M | 158 | 32,491 | 25 | 32 |
| GPT-2 Medium | 355M | 410 | 231,877 | 15 | 16 |
| TinyLlama-1.1B | 1.1B | 728 | 742,996 | 10 | 4 |
| Phi-1.5 | 1.3B | 794 | 886,597 | 7 | 2 |

**Training configuration:** AdamW optimizer (beta1=0.9, beta2=0.95, epsilon=1e-6), weight decay 0.1, constant learning rate without warmup, gradient accumulation every 4 steps, trained on 2 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Learning rates: 1e-3 for GPT-2 models, 4e-5 for TinyLlama, 2e-4 for Phi-1.5.

---

### Dataset Construction

The authors construct **synthetic biographical data** using ChatGPT to generate fictional entities, ensuring the knowledge was never present in the models' pre-training corpora.

**Knowledge representation:** Factual knowledge as triples: **(subject, relation, attribute)**
- **Subjects:** Names in "first_name middle_name last_name" format
- **Relations:** Birth date, city, major, university, company
- **Attributes:** Randomly sampled from pools (e.g., 30x12x126 combinations for dates)
- **Templates:** 50 natural language variations per attribute type

**Corpus statistics:**
- 50,000 total entities
- 133,408 biography segments
- 10 million tokens total
- Average segment length: 76.8 tokens
- Frequency distribution: Exponential (1-27 occurrences)

**Knowledge classification (two dimensions):**

*By relevance (1:4 ratio):*
- **K_rel (Relevant new knowledge):** Extensions of existing knowledge -- new relations for known entities (e.g., using Wikipedia celebrity names as subjects, so the model already knows something about the subject)
- **K_compl (Completely new knowledge):** Entirely novel fictional entities with no pre-existing knowledge

*By frequency:*
- Low-freq: 1 occurrence [1,2)
- Medium-freq: 2-5 occurrences [2,5]
- High-freq: >5 occurrences (5,27]

---

### The Formation-to-Optimization Phase Shift

The paper identifies a **distinct two-phase pattern** in circuit evolution, detected through converging signals:

**Phase transition points (model-specific):**
- GPT-2 Small: Epoch 7
- GPT-2 Medium: Epoch 4
- TinyLlama: Epoch 1
- Phi-1.5: Epoch 1

(Larger models transition earlier, suggesting pre-existing representational capacity accelerates circuit formation.)

**Formation Phase characteristics:**
- **Circuit Entropy:** Rapid decrease -- edge importance scores become more concentrated as the circuit structure crystallizes
- **Structural Consistency:** Monotonic upward trend in Jaccard Similarity between intermediate and final checkpoint circuit topologies
- **Topology:** Unstable; critical edges and nodes are still being incorporated
- **Performance (Hit@10):** Gradual, slow improvement
- **Component activity:** Mover heads emerge, relation heads decrease in mid-to-deeper layers

**Optimization Phase characteristics:**
- **Circuit Entropy:** Downward trend slows significantly -- topology has stabilized
- **Topology:** Core architecture established and stable
- **Performance (Hit@10):** Rapid improvement despite topology stabilization -- the circuit is now being *refined* rather than *built*
- **Component activity:** Specialized head proportions stabilize; internal computations are refined

**Key quantitative finding:** Circuits aligned with post-phase-shift topologies ultimately perform, on average, **54% better** than those aligned with pre-phase-shift topologies, indicating the structural reorganization at the transition point is critical to performance.

**Metrics used:**
- **Knowledge Circuit Entropy:** H(C) = -sum(P(e) log P(e)), where P(e) normalizes edge importance scores -- measures edge importance concentration
- **Jaccard Similarity:** Measures edge/node set overlap between intermediate and final checkpoints
- **Hit@10:** Whether the correct attribute token ranks in the top 10 predicted tokens

---

### The Deep-to-Shallow Pattern

Circuit evolution progresses systematically from deeper to shallower network layers:

**During the Formation Phase (early training):**
- **Mid-to-deeper layers:** Emergence of "mover heads" (specialized attention heads facilitating subject-attribute information movement) from nearly zero. Simultaneous decrease in relation head proportion.
- **Lower layers:** Relative stability; edge activation ratios gradually decrease.
- Edge activation ratios in mid-to-deeper layers exhibit corresponding increases.

**During the Optimization Phase (later training):**
- **Lower layers:** Progressive enrichment of knowledge representations
- **Mid-to-deeper layers:** Stabilization of extraction functions
- Edge activation ratios stabilize across all layers

**Specialized attention head types analyzed:**
- **Mover heads:** Move relevant information (subject to attribute) through attention
- **Relation heads:** Extract attributes for subjects
- **Mixture heads:** Combine information from both functions

**Edge Activation Ratio:** Proportion of edges originating from each layer within the circuit, relative to all possible edges from that layer -- used to track the layer-wise evolution pattern.

---

### How New Knowledge Acquisition Depends on Relevance to Existing Knowledge

The paper demonstrates that **K_rel (relevant new knowledge) is consistently acquired more efficiently than K_compl (completely new knowledge):**

- The K_rel performance curve (Hit@10) consistently lies above the K_compl curve across all models and throughout training
- This holds across different frequency categories
- The authors interpret this as LLMs exhibiting "preferential learning efficiency when assimilating knowledge extensions within existing conceptual frameworks, as opposed to acquiring completely new knowledge"
- The mechanism is attributed to the model's ability to "integrate new information more efficiently" when building upon pre-existing parametric knowledge structures

This finding is validated at both the **whole model level** (overall accuracy) and the **circuit level** (circuit-specific Hit@10).

---

### Limitations (as stated by the authors)

1. **Architecture scope:** Only decoder-only Transformers are studied. Encoder-decoder and encoder-only architectures are excluded.

2. **Model scale:** Analysis is limited to models of 1.3B parameters or fewer. The authors cite computational resource constraints and note that their circuit discovery methods (EAP-IG) are unsuitable for larger models using Grouped Query Attention (GQA). However, they reference prior work suggesting "circuit analyses conducted on small models provide insights that still apply over model scales."

3. **Training technique:** Only standard next-token prediction is used as the training objective. The paper does not analyze the impact of instruction-tuning, RLHF, or specialized continual pre-training methods. The authors acknowledge "numerous studies focus on designing novel training techniques to enhance efficiency."

---

### Reviewer Comments

**No public reviews were found.** ACL 2025 uses the ACL Rolling Review (ARR) system via OpenReview, but the reviews for this specific paper do not appear to be publicly accessible through search. The OpenReview forum page is JavaScript-rendered and could not be accessed programmatically. No substantive community discussion was found on HuggingFace, Twitter/X, or other platforms beyond descriptive summaries (e.g., the Moonlight.io literature review page, which provides only an expository summary without critique).

---

### Summary of Key Contributions

This paper is notable for being one of the first to apply **mechanistic interpretability (circuit analysis)** to study the *dynamics* of knowledge acquisition during continual pre-training, rather than analyzing circuits at a single snapshot. The three findings -- relevance-dependent acquisition, formation-to-optimization phase shift, and deep-to-shallow evolution -- provide a structured framework for understanding how factual knowledge becomes embedded in transformer architectures over the course of training.

1. **Activation Collection (Stage 1):** Instances where knowledge conflicts occur are separated into two behavioral groups: D_C (model generates contextual answers) and D_M (model generates parametric/memorized answers). - **Addition constraint (Eq. 3):** z_i^+ = max{z_{Mi} - z_i, 0} -- prevents overshooting the target activation level.

- **Add only:** Adds parametric features without removing contextual ones. Performs worse than uncontrolled baseline.

**Venue:** ICML 2025 (Spotlight), PMLR Volume 267, pp. 34074-34104
**ArXiv:** 2503.10996 (v1: March 14, 2025; v2: June 6, 2025)

---

### Full Abstract

In this study, we go beyond this fundamental assumption by uncovering a critical phenomenon we term the superposition of contextual information and parametric memory, where highly influential attention heads simultaneously contribute to both memory and context. ---

1. **Enhancing parametric beliefs:** The input context is potentially misleading; the LM is treated as an oracle that should rely on its internal knowledge.
2. **Enhancing contextual reliance:** The input context is accurate but the LM's prior knowledge may be outdated; the model should prioritize context.

They formalize the causal analysis measurement as:

**E_{(x,y)}[ P(y | x, do(M^(i) = alpha * M^(i))) - P(y | x) ]** (Equation 1)

where M^(i) is a specific model component with index i, alpha is a scaling factor, and y is set to either y_p (parametric answer) or y_c (contextual answer) depending on the goal.

---

### Discovery of Head Superposition (Section 3.1)

This is the paper's key mechanistic insight. They examined the effect of knocking out (zero-ablating) each component across three scenarios on the World Capital dataset with Gemma-2b:
- **Clean inputs (no conflict):** Removing nearly all components *decreased* parametric answer probability
- **Substitution conflicts:** Removing components led to *both* increases and decreases
- **Coherent conflicts:** Removing nearly all components *increased* parametric answer probability

Quantitatively, the number of components yielding consistent parametric gains across all three conflict types was: **0 out of 26 for entire layers, 1 for MLP modules, and only 6 for attention modules** (out of 26 layers in Gemma).

The critical finding from Table 1: When they ranked the top-4 "memory heads" by their effectiveness in substitution conflicts, **half of them showed the opposite effect** in coherent conflicts. Specifically:
- Head (8,0): +0.18 context prob increase in subs-conflict, but +0.04 context prob increase in coh-conflict (opposite of desired)
- Head (9,3): +0.13 context prob increase in subs-conflict, but **-0.17** context prob (i.e., became a context head) in coh-conflict
- Head (13,5): +0.11 context prob in subs-conflict, but **-0.13** in coh-conflict

This demonstrates that "the same model component may exhibit different influences on parametric and contextual knowledge depending on residual streams received from prior layers."

Even when individual head interventions are effective, combining them can backfire. Table 2 shows this clearly with target probability values when combining top-ranked heads under coherent conflict:
- None (original model): 0.03
- Top 1 head: 0.12
- Top 3 heads: 0.24
- Top 10 heads: **0.14** (degraded from Top 3!)

This reveals that "different modules can 'counteract' each other, even though individual intervention contributes to substantial performance gains." The likely cause: modified activations from earlier layers alter downstream behavior due to the residual stream dependency.

These two observations collectively reveal what the authors term **"CP superposition" (superposition of contextual information and parametric memory)** -- the roles of "context" or "memory" of model components depend on the inputs they receive, not on fixed head specialization.

JuICE (Just Run Twice) operates in two stages:

**Stage 1: Head Identification**

The goal is to find two sets of attention heads: S_1 (heads with positive scaling effect -- to be amplified) and S_2 (heads with negative scaling effect -- to be suppressed).

The algorithm (Algorithm 1 + Algorithm 2 in Appendix E) works as follows:

1. **Input:** Model M, a small head selection dataset D (|D| = 4 samples by default), sets of positive scaling factors alpha+ = {alpha_j} and negative scaling factors alpha- = {alpha_j'}.

2. **Score computation (Algorithm 2):** For each sample (X,y) in D, each conflict type j, each head H_i, and each scaling coefficient alpha_i:
   - Compute: S+_i[j][i] += P_y((M | Do(H_i = H_i + alpha_i * H_i))(x)) - P_y(M(x))
   - Similarly for S-_i[j][i] with negative scaling

3. **Filter inconsistent heads (Algorithm 3):** For each conflict type j and each head i:
   - If S+[j][i] < 0 for any j, remove i from H+ (positive head candidates)
   - If S-[j][i] < 0 for any j, remove i from H- (negative head candidates)
   - This ensures **consistency across ALL conflict types** -- only heads that maintain non-negative scores across all types survive.

4. **Aggregate and select:** Sum scores across conflict types: S_i+ = sum_j S+[j][i]. Select top K heads by aggregated score. In practice, K = 5 for smaller models (Gemma, Phi2, StableLm2), K = 10 for larger models (Llama2, Llama3, Olmo).

5. **Scaling factor tuning:** alpha+ is tuned from {0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5} and alpha- from {0, -1, -2, -3} using validation.

This is the core innovation that addresses the counteracting effects:

1. **First run:** Feed input x into model M normally. For each attention head H_l in the selected sets S_1 or S_2, **save** its output: Aux[l] = H_l.

   - If l is in S_2: H_l <- H_l + beta- * Aux[l] (add scaled first-run activation with negative factor)

The key intuition: "The first-run activations serve as more reliable steering directions." Because the first run is unperturbed, its head outputs reflect the natural processing of the input. When these saved activations are added during the second run, they provide consistent directional guidance that avoids the cascade of counteracting effects seen in single-pass interventions.

**Parametric Knowledge Setting (6 datasets, the "ParaConflict" benchmark):**

  - Type 2 (Substitution): e.g., "The name of the capital city of France is Beijing. The name of the capital city of France is"

- JuICE: Type 1 = 79.1%, Type 2 = 75.3%, Type 3 = **73.4%**

The theory uses a simplified two-layer attention-only transformer with one head per layer, absolute positional encoding, and residual connections.

2. **Induction** (contextual): Learn to predict token b following the pattern [... q, b, ..., q] -> b

**Proposition 5.2 (Existence of a Perfect Solver):** There exists a two-layer transformer that can solve both tasks with perfect accuracy. The construction explicitly gives:
- Layer 1 W_KQ^(1) = C * sum_{t=1}^{T-1} p_t * p_{t+1}^T (implements "copy from previous embedding")
- Layer 2 W_KQ^(2) = C_1 * (W_OV^1 * phi(q)) * phi(q)^T + C_2 * sum_{s in S} phi(s) * phi(q)^T
- Layer 2 W_OV^(2) = C_3 * sum_{k in N} mu(k) * phi(k)^T + C_4 * sum_{s in S} mu(G*(s)) * phi(s)^T

The second layer's W_OV^(2) **inherently forms a superposition** -- the C_3 term handles the induction task (copying noise tokens) while the C_4 term handles factual recall. Both coexist in the same weight matrix.

- Single-pass deletion removes both heads, giving random guessing

3. **Domain generality:** "The parametric and contextual answer may not be always distinct under more abstract domains as we discussed in this work. Extending our method to these complex cases and settings remains an important direction for future research."

4. **Theoretical simplifications:** The theoretical analysis uses a simplified two-layer transformer with single attention heads and linear attention assumptions, which "doesn't capture full model complexity."

- **Gaps noted:** Lack of discussion of computational overhead from dual-pass inference; limited analysis of failure cases or boundary conditions; generalization to other model types remains unclear

Here is my thorough research report on "Summing Up the Facts: Additive Mechanisms Behind Factual Recall in LLMs" by Bilal Chughtai, Alan Cooney, and Neel Nanda.

---

## Full Abstract

"How do transformer-based large language models (LLMs) store and retrieve knowledge? We focus on the most basic form of this task -- factual recall, where the model is tasked with explicitly surfacing stored facts in prompts of form 'Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of'. We find that the mechanistic story behind factual recall is more complex than previously thought. It comprises several distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms that additively combine, constructively interfering on the correct attribute. We term this generic phenomena the additive motif: models compute through summing up multiple independent contributions. Each mechanism's contribution may be insufficient alone, but summing results in constructive interference on the correct answer. In addition, we extend the method of direct logit attribution to attribute an attention head's output to individual source tokens. We use this technique to unpack what we call 'mixed heads' -- which are themselves a pair of two separate additive updates from different source tokens."

---

## Publication Venue

Despite the user's reference to NeurIPS 2024, the paper was actually presented as a **poster at the NeurIPS 2023 "Attributing Model Behaviour at Scale" (ATTRIB) Workshop**. It was also submitted to **ICLR 2024** (submission #9284, under the "Generative models" primary area), though the outcome of that submission is unclear from public records. The arXiv preprint was posted February 2024 (arXiv:2402.07321). As of the Google Scholar profile, the paper has **40 citations**.

---

## Model and Dataset

- **Primary model studied:** **Pythia-2.8B** (a transformer-based LLM from the Pythia suite by EleutherAI)
- **Generalization:** Similar mechanisms were found in **GPT-2 XL**, **GPT-J**, and other **Pythia models** of varying sizes
- **Task setup:** Factual recall using tuples *(s, r, a)* -- subject, relation, attribute -- in prompts like "Fact: The Colosseum is in the country of [Italy]"
- **Success metric:** The correct attribute being within the **top ten output logits**
- **Token positions analyzed:** PREFIX, SUBJECT, RELATION, and END (last token position where prediction is made)

---

## The Additive Motif -- Core Discovery

The central finding is what they call the **additive motif**: factual recall is not achieved by a single dominant mechanism, but rather by **four distinct, independent, and qualitatively different mechanisms** that each contribute partial, individually insufficient signals to the residual stream. When these contributions are **summed** (as they naturally are in the residual stream of a transformer), they **constructively interfere** on the correct attribute token, boosting it above competing tokens in the output logits.

This is a key insight about how transformers compute: the architecture's linear residual stream acts as a natural summing channel, enabling independent circuits to contribute additively without needing to coordinate.

---

## The Four Mechanisms

### 1. Subject Heads (~18% contribution)
- **Definition:** Attention heads that primarily attend to the **SUBJECT tokens** at the last token position
- **Behavior:** Extract attributes associated with the subject entity, even if the specific relation in the prompt does not directly call for those attributes. They activate in response to any factual recall prompt containing that subject.
- **Example:** Given "The Colosseum is in the country of," subject heads would extract various attributes of "The Colosseum" (location, age, type, etc.)

### 2. Relation Heads (~24% contribution)
- **Definition:** Attention heads that attend strongly to the **RELATION tokens**
- **Behavior:** Extract many attributes associated with the given relation, regardless of the specific subject. They boost tokens that are common answers to a given type of relation.
- **Example:** For "is in the country of," relation heads would boost country names generally

### 3. Mixed Heads (~27% contribution)
- **Definition:** Attention heads that attend to **both SUBJECT and RELATION tokens** simultaneously
- **Behavior:** These are the most sophisticated heads -- they extract the **correct attribute** from subject tokens while simultaneously extracting relation-related attributes from relation tokens. The paper's key methodological contribution is showing that mixed heads are themselves decomposable into **two separate additive updates from different source tokens**
- **Key insight:** Using the extended DLA (see below), mixed heads can be unpacked into a subject-attending component and a relation-attending component, each making an independent additive contribution

### 4. MLPs (~30% contribution)
- **Definition:** The feed-forward (MLP) layers of the transformer
- **Behavior:** Boost many attributes related to the relation, without necessarily prioritizing the correct attribute. They provide a broad, relation-contextual boost
- **Note:** MLPs are described as boosting relevant attributes more diffusely compared to the more targeted attention head mechanisms

---

## Methodological Details

### Direct Logit Attribution (DLA)
The standard DLA technique projects a component's output through the unembedding matrix to see its contribution to output logits:

- **Logit lens:** pi_t^l = LayerNorm(z_t^l) * W_U, where z_t^l is the residual stream activation at layer l and token position t, and W_U is the unembedding matrix
- **DLA for individual heads:** pi_t^{l,h} = LayerNorm(a_h(z_t^{l-1})) * W_U, where a_h is the attention head output function

### Extended DLA by Source Token (Key Methodological Contribution)
The paper's main technical contribution is decomposing an attention head's output by which **source token** contributed the information. Since an attention head's output is a **linear weighted sum over source positions**:

- The head output can be written as: sum_k attn_prob^{l-1,k} * LayerNorm(z_k^{l-1}) * W_V * W_O
- This enables **DLA by source token**: pi_t^{l,h,k} = LayerNorm(attn_prob^{l-1,k} * LayerNorm(z_k^{l-1}) * W_V * W_O) * W_U

This decomposition allows attributing how much of a head's logit contribution comes from attending to SUBJECT tokens vs. RELATION tokens vs. other positions. This is how they disentangle mixed heads into their constituent additive components.

### Activation Patching / Edge Patching
The paper employs **edge patching** -- ablating the direct path between specific model components and the logits to measure causal importance. By ablating individual mechanisms and observing the drop in performance, they confirm the independence and additive nature of the four mechanisms.

### Counterfactual Analysis
They define counterfactual sets to characterize each mechanism's behavior:
- **S-set:** Attributes relevant to the subject (obtained by varying the relation while keeping the subject fixed)
- **R-set:** Attributes relevant to the relation (obtained by varying the subject while keeping the relation fixed)

---

## How Constructive Interference Works

The key quantitative insight is that each mechanism alone produces an **insufficient** boost to the correct attribute. However:

1. Subject heads boost subject-related attributes (including the correct one among many)
2. Relation heads boost relation-related attributes (including the correct one among many)
3. Mixed heads contribute more targeted boosts from both subject and relation information
4. MLPs provide broad relation-contextual boosts

When summed in the residual stream, the correct attribute is the **only token that receives boosting from ALL four mechanisms simultaneously**, while incorrect tokens only receive boosting from a subset. This selective overlap creates constructive interference specifically on the correct answer.

---

The paper builds on and extends several key lines of research:
- **Meng et al. (2022/2023)** -- ROME and Causal Tracing: locating factual associations in GPT, showing MLP layers store factual knowledge
- **Geva et al. (2023)** -- Dissecting recall of factual associations, identifying the role of attention heads in attribute extraction
- **Nanda et al.** -- Prior mechanistic interpretability work on factual recall
- The paper's contribution is showing that these previously identified components (MLPs, various attention heads) are not the full story individually but rather combine additively in a previously unappreciated way

Unfortunately, **no public reviewer comments were accessible**. The OpenReview page for the ICLR 2024 submission (id: P2gnDEHGu3) shows only metadata and the abstract -- the review content was not publicly available through web fetching. 2. **Narrow task scope:** The paper studies only simple factual recall prompts of the form "The X is in the country of" -- not complex multi-hop reasoning or implicit knowledge use
